en: Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Master Xuansha:

I have heard that there is no falling into stages or ranks. He entrusted [his disciples] with these words: "Go well; seek and contemplate. This penetrates the golden needle through and through, yet one did not expect the carrying pole to break midway.
As soon as the single robe was spread out, he said, "I dare not deceive myself. Ordinary and holy are both eliminated; this is the direction within the breast.

As the water flowed out, he struck his toe, and thereupon attained sudden enlightenment regarding the non-arising of suffering and pleasure. When pressed with questions on the spot, he declared, "This has nothing to do with the Western Land.

Thus we know that the Dharma-treasury has its foundation and that the life-blood of the lineage is transmitted from one to another. Lately, those who lead and teach in various quarters have no authentic model for their teacher-disciple relationship;
those who discourse on Chan have not yet met the standard for leaving the world, yet they claim to have realized the Way and recklessly presume to guide others.

When one investigates the origin of this [transmission], there is nothing specific to point to. Yet, reflecting back upon the past, the Great Master Xuansha distantly inherited the lineage from Vulture Peak and directly received it from Caoxi;
he was the close grandson of Shitou and the true son of Xuefeng, his mind-seal transmitted through the successive patriarchs.
His teachings permeated the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. When a fierce tiger appeared before him, he spoke directly, saying, "This is your dead snake being playfully handled.

He did not yield to his master; thus, many eminent scholars from all quarters came to resolve their doubts with him. From Japan and Korea, people traveled ten thousand *li* to seek his instruction. I was born in this degenerate age, far removed from ancient times.
In the past, when I entered Min Province, I once inquired about ancient monasteries; the stupas appear as they did yesterday, and the stone pillars still remain.

I remain here, my heart filled with grief; there is no ground upon which to rest it, and how could I wish to stay? I am delighted that the layman Xilin Deshan has renovated this historic site and collected the Master’s teachings.

He has sent a messenger to Yue to request that I provide a preface for them. Yet, considering myself a person of shallow learning and mediocre intellect, with dull faculties and slow thought, I can only briefly set forth the general outline to be circulated for future generations.
As for the profound and mysterious wind of the Dharma and its wondrous purport, these are fully contained within the book itself.
This involves the ancient verses and the critical comments of others, extending even beyond the recorded texts. Following the Middle and the Extremes, one tastes the honey;

the jeweled nets interlace their light. If one were to raise the whip without blinking, one would still be lost even upon face-to-face encounter. Yet, once it has entered one's hands, one immediately knows that the ancients are as if present.
Awakening must arise from conditions; the record is likewise not merely letters.
Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Xuansha, composed and carved by Sanmu Zhanran Yuancheng, Abbot of Yunmen Monastery in Dongyue,
during the late spring of the Bingyin year of the Tianqi era.
When I first began to study Buddhism, I took pleasure in the sayings of the Chan school, and my appreciation for Xuan Sha was particularly great.
Upon his curved wooden seat, he was like a jar atop a house, or a bird flying through the sky—leaving no trace behind at all. He would have the reader recite a passage once;

then, like a "resonant insect," he would call out whatever the reader had forgotten, immediately silencing them. At that time, I engaged in this vigorous exchange with a multitude of seven hundred people.
In his deeds, he revitalized the lineage of Shitou and humbled the transmission of Fayan. Thus, within the gate of Xuefeng, it was through Xuansha that the Way attained even greater honor.
Monks from all quarters, as well as those from Japan and Goryeo, all flocked to him to resolve their doubts regarding the kōans and the pivot of his teaching style;
his school flourished to the height of its glory during that era. Formerly, there were the "Great" and "Small" Records (Dalu and Xiaolu) circulating in the world.

Now, none of these remain extant. During my leisure time while dwelling in the mountains, I have searched through various collections and compiled them into three fascicles to present to Master Yunmen.
The Master composed a preface and put them into circulation. Indeed, when the "poison-dust" drum is struck but once, all who hear it perish.
It makes no distinction between near and far. It has been seven hundred years since the Master departed. Is there not anyone today who, upon hearing [his words], passes away?
Every single character and every single phrase is the sound of the "poison-coated drum. As the Duke Li Zhongding said: "Do not say that the fisherman has already become silent;
even now, his preaching of the Dharma resounds like thunder. To take the arm of the ancients and to uproot and establish the present—this is [the way].
This carving of the record is truly indispensable.
Recorded with incense burning in reverence by the Layman Lin Hongyan of Mount De in Minzhong at the Monastery on Zhongshan.
*The Record of Chan Master Zongyi of Xuansha, Fuzhou*, Volume One.
Compiled by the Layman Shanzhong De, Lin Hongyan. The Master’s name was Shibei.
He was a native of Min County, Fuzhou, and belonged to the Xie clan. From his youth, he enjoyed fishing; he would launch a small skiff upon the Nantai River and associate with fishermen.
At the beginning of the Xiantong era of the Tang dynasty, when he was just thirty years old, he suddenly developed a longing to transcend the mundane world.
He then abandoned his fishing boat and went to the Chan Master Lingxun of Furuang to shave his head. He proceeded to Kaiyuan Temple in Yuzhang to receive full ordination from Vinaya Master Daoxuan.
Wearing coarse cloth robes and straw sandals, he took only enough food to sustain his breath; he frequently sat in meditation throughout the entire day, which all marveled at.
Although he and Xuefeng Yicun were originally brothers in the same Dharma lineage, they related to one another with the intimacy of teacher and disciple. Xuefeng...

Because of his ascetic practices, he was called Dharma Master Toudo. One day, wishing to travel throughout all quarters to seek out spiritual friends, he took up his bag and set out over the mountain pass.
His foot struck a stone, drawing blood and causing him intense pain. He sighed and said, "This body does not truly exist;
from where does this pain arise? He then returned to Xuefeng. One day, Xuefeng asked, "Which one is Dharma Master Beidou? He replied, "I truly do not dare."
He deceived people. On another day, Xuefeng summoned him, saying, "Head-Taoist Bei, why do you not go on a pilgrimage to study everywhere?
The Master replied, "Bodhidharma did not come to the Eastern Land; the Second Patriarch did not go to the Western Heaven. Xuefeng approved of this. (Verse: Suddenly kicking it over, he knew to rest;
the green mountains of Baiyue he no longer roams. From then on, the moon upon the rivers of Fujian has shone empty until now, illuminating the fisherman’s hook.)
The Fisherman’s Boat. The Buddha-land is white; on the fishing boat is Old Third Lang. He has kicked over Mount Sumeru and returned to his native land.

He must surely laugh at the traveler who has not yet returned, lonesome and lodging abroad in a foreign land. One Original Awakening. Without leaving the guesthouse in Min, he has already returned home.
As soon as he mounts the soaring vulture, his eyes grow dim. One can only laugh at Master Zeng for being so cruel-hearted; he let go of old Xu with a light bamboo cane.
Sha (Dun’an Yan). Upon ascending Mount Xianggu, he collaborated with the Master in the construction [of the monastery]. Disciples from afar flocked there;
the Master would enter the inner quarters to seek resolution from him, never flagging from morning until night. Furthermore, he studied the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and realized the nature of the mind.

Consequently, his responses to stimuli were swift and nimble, and they accorded perfectly with the *Sūtras*. Whenever scholars from various regions encountered points they could not resolve, they would invariably seek [his guidance].
As for his requests for further instruction, even when engaging in dialectical inquiry with Master Xuefeng, he did not shrink from the role of the benevolent one.
Xuefeng said, "Tuduo Bei is a man who has returned for a second birth."

Ascending the hall, he said: "All you practitioners of Chan: you have all come from traveling in various directions, claiming that you are practicing Chan and studying the Way because there is some extraordinary place to go.
Or do you simply go about asking questions here and there? If there is such a thing, try to demonstrate it."
I shall bear witness for you. Is this something that can be fully known through consciousness? Is there anyone here?
If there is not, you should know that you are merely chasing after profit. Since you have all come here, I now ask you: do you people possess eyes?
If it exists, you ought to recognize it right now. Do you recognize it?
If you do not recognize it, I shall call you a person born blind and deaf—is that so? Are you willing to speak thus? Zen practitioners, do not humiliate yourselves.
This is your true reality. When have you ever been such a person? The Buddhas of the ten directions place you upon their crowns, not daring to let even a single hair’s breadth of error occur.
They merely say that this matter can only be known by me. Do you understand?
Now, as we continue the succession, everyone says they inherit from Śākyamuni; I say that Śākyamuni and I are fellow practitioners. You—speak! What do you practice?
"Who is it? Do you understand? It is not at all easy to know. Only through great awakening can one truly come to know it.
If it were merely a matter of limited realization, it could not be perceived by you. Do you recognize what 'great awakening' is?
It is not for you to recognize its reflecting clarity before a skull; nor is it for you to speak of emptiness or non-existence, or of this side and that side. There is a world...
Regarding worldly dharmas: there is one thing that is not a worldly dharma. You sons of the patriarchs, even empty space arises from delusive illusion.

If you were to be thoroughly awakened right now, where would there be anything to speak of? Since there is not even a trace of empty space, where could there be the sequence of karma within the three realms?
Birth is conditioned by parents; they establish for you the notions of before and after. Right now—
To say that the Way does not exist is already a deceptive word; how much more so to claim it exists? Do you understand?
You monks who have long been traveling on pilgrimage call yourselves those who possess awakening. Now I ask you:

in a place such as a steep mountain or a precipitous cliff, utterly remote from human habitation, is there still Buddha-dharma? Can you discern it? If you cannot discern it, you are by no means yet finished. I...
In the ordinary way, before the deceased monk is precisely awakening (bodhi) encountered at every turn. That divine light extending ten thousand miles is the mark behind the crown of the head.
If one can perceive it, one will be able to emerge from the realm of shadows and cast off the conceptual thoughts before the skull.
It all comes down to nothing other than your own true, substantial human body. Where else could there be another dharma capable of covering you? Do you know? Do you understand? Still?
"Do you believe this? Can you take responsibility for it? You must exert great effort. Ascending the hall, he said:
"The Buddha-way is vast and open; there are no set paths. It is the gateless gate of liberation, the mindless mind of the Way-man.

It does not reside within the three periods of time, and thus it cannot be elevated or depressed. To establish it would deviate from the Truth; it does not belong to the realm of creation. Movement..."

If one moves, the root of birth and death arises; if one remains still, one becomes intoxicated in the realm of dullness and torpor. If both movement and stillness are extinguished, one falls into a void;
if both movement and stillness are grasped, one is deluded regarding Buddha-nature. One must, in the face of sensory objects and conditions, be like withered wood and cold ashes.
Applied temporarily, it does not lose its appropriateness. A mirror reflects all images without confusing its radiance; a bird flies through the air without mixing with the color of space.

Thus, throughout the ten directions there are no reflected images, and within the three realms there are no traces of movement. One does not fall into the mechanism of coming and going, nor does one abide in a middle state of mind.
Within the bell there is no sound of the drum; within the drum there is no sound of the bell. The bell and the drum do not [interfere with one another].
Interconnected. Every phrase is without before or after. Like a strong man extending his arm, he does not rely on the power of others.
Like a lion roaming, how could he seek a companion? In the nine heavens, all obscurations are severed; where is there a need for piercing through?

This single segment of luminosity has never been dimmed. If you arrive here, the essence is tranquil and eternally distinct. The sun blazes with brilliance, beyond all bounds. Within the space of perfect enlightenment, it is not...

Shaking and moving; swallowing and blazing through heaven and earth, shining forth in utter transcendence. Now, as for the Buddha appearing in the world: fundamentally, there is no coming or going. Names and forms have no substance;

the Way is originally suchness (*tathatā*). Reality is naturally so by its own nature; it does not depend on cultivation or realization. The essential point is empty stillness, yet its functioning is never obscured. It does not involve the mud of worldly dust.
Within this, even a hair’s breadth cannot be fully described—were one to do so, they would become a member of the retinue of Māra. Thus says the verse:

The preceding phrase follows upon the subsequent one; this is the difficult point for those in training. Thus, a single phrase can encompass the whole of heaven, and through the eighty thousand gates, birth and death are forever severed.

Even if one attains a state like the moon’s reflection in an autumn pond or the sound of a bell in a silent night—unimpaired by being struck and undispersed when touching the waves—it remains merely a matter on the shore of birth and death. Where a man of the Way proceeds, he is like fire melting ice.

In the end, it never solidifies into ice. Once an arrow has left the bowstring, it possesses no momentum to return. Thus, it refuses to dwell within its cage; though called out, it does not turn its head.
The ancient sages made no arrangements for it, and to this day it has no fixed location. If one reaches this point, one ascends the profound with every step;

it belongs neither to the heterodox nor the orthodox. Consciousness cannot perceive it, and wisdom cannot know it. To move is to lose what is appropriate; to awaken— [Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]
This immediately confuses the fundamental meaning; the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas tremble with fear, and those on the ten stages of the bodhisattva path are struck with terror.

The pathways of speech are cut off, and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished. Thus, Śākyamuni was forced to close his room in Magadha, Vimalakīrti remained silent in Vaiśālī, Subhūti proclaimed "non-speaking" to manifest the Way, and Śakra and Brahmā ceased their listening as flowers rained down. If it is thus, what more is there to doubt before one's very eyes?
There is no place of dwelling; it transcends past, present, and future, defying all limitations and boundaries. The paths of thought and intellect are cut off;
it is not produced by adornment, being primordially true and pure. Whether in movement, speech, or laughter, it is clearly manifest wherever one is, lacking nothing whatsoever.

People of the present age do not speak of this underlying principle, but instead recklessly involve themselves in worldly affairs and sensory dust. Thus they become stained and attached everywhere, bound at every turn—even as they...

Upon awakening, one realizes that the sensory realms are chaotic and that names and forms are unreal; thus, one intends to settle the mind and withdraw thoughts, to subsume phenomena within emptiness.
Yet, even with eyes closed and pupils hidden, thoughts inevitably arise. One must repeatedly break them down; as soon as subtle perceptions emerge, they must be immediately suppressed.
To hold such a view is to be a non-Buddhist who has fallen into nihilism, a walking corpse whose soul has not yet departed.
It is a state of dark obscurity, devoid of awareness or cognition—like one who plugs their ears to steal a bell, merely deceiving themselves. To make such distinctions here is incorrect.
This is not a matter of hiding behind doors or lurking in corners; every word is manifest before us. It cannot be deliberated upon and does not involve literary artifice.

Fundamentally, it is severed from the realm of dust; fundamentally, there are no stages or positions. It is provisionally called "a child who has left the home-life," yet in the end, there is no trace.
Whether True Suchness, ordinary beings, sages, those in hell, or humans and devas—these are merely expedient methods for healing the mad child. Even empty space itself undergoes no change.
How could the Great Way have rising or sinking? If one awakens, then whether moving freely or acting spontaneously, one does not depart from the fundamental limit (*mūlapada*).

If one reaches this point, there is no place for either ordinary beings or sages to stand. If you direct your attention toward the words, you will be drowned and destroyed; if you run outward in pursuit, you will likewise be lost.

Furthermore, one falls into the realm of Māra. As for "suchness" (tathatā) ascending upward, there is nothing that can be contrived; it is just like a blazing furnace that harbors no mosquitoes or gnats.
This principle is fundamentally level and plain—what need is there to scrape it away? Whether moving or still, whether raising an eyebrow or not, this is the true path of liberation.

Do not forcibly employ mental calculations; to establish such constructs is to deviate from the truth. If you reach this point, not even a hair’s breadth shall be accepted; to point toward it with the intellect is already an error.
"Even if a thousand sages were to appear, not a single word could be placed [upon this].
Long standing; take care. Ascending the hall, he said: "I now ask you all: what matter can you take up and bear? In what world do you establish yourself and find your livelihood?
Can you discern this? If you cannot discern it, it is just like seeing flowers in the air when one rubs one's eyes—seeing things that are not there."
It was immediately cured. Do you understand? What you now see—the mountains, rivers, and the great earth; form and emptiness, light and darkness;

all these various things—are all but the phantom flowers of a deluded labor. To call them such is called inverted perception. Now, as for those who have left the household life, they recognize the mind and penetrate the source;
therefore, they are called śramaṇas. Since you have now shaved your hair, donned the robes, and assumed the appearance of a śramaṇa, you should immediately—
There is the distinction between benefiting oneself and benefiting others. At present, it is as if you are looking at a vast expanse of pitch-black ink;
you cannot even save yourself, so how could you possibly know how to benefit others? O Benevolent One, the matters concerning the causal conditions of the Buddha-dharma are of great importance.

Do not treat them with indifference or engage in idle chatter and superficial talk with one another. Do not let the time slip away by seeking mere profit; for time is difficult to obtain and truly precious.
Great man, why do you not examine within yourself to see what this matter truly is? As for the ancestral vehicle of the Buddhas from of old—it is the crown lineage of all Buddhas.
Since you are unable to take responsibility for it, I have therefore used skillful means to exhort you:
simply follow the gate of Kāśyapa and proceed directly beyond. This one gate transcends the cause and effect of ordinary beings and sages; it transcends the wondrous [realm] of Vairocana.

Adorning the ocean of worlds, this transcends the expedient gates of other Śākyamunis. Directly beneath, throughout eternal kalpas, not a single thing has been taught to you to serve as an object for the eyes to see.
Why do you not urgently investigate and grasp it yourself? It is not that one must say, "I shall wait for three or two lifetimes to accumulate pure karma over a long period.
O worthy one, what is the matter of the *zong* (the fundamental vehicle)? It cannot be attained through your own contrived efforts.
One may depart by means of skillful adornment, but one cannot depart by means of the knowledge of others' minds or the recollection of past lives. Do you understand? Consider this:

when Śākyamuni appeared in the world, he performed all manner of transformations and preached the twelve divisions of the teachings like pouring water from one vessel into another, creating a grand display of Buddhist activity.
Yet, within this very gate, not a single point of that can be used; not even a hair’s breadth of such artifice will do.
Do you understand? It is like a dream-event, and it is also like the talk of one asleep. A śramaṇa should not show his head;
it is not the same as a dream-event, for it is because he has recognized it. Do you understand? To recognize it is to be a person of great liberation and great penetration.

Therefore, he transcends the ordinary and surpasses the sages; he is born beyond birth and leaves death behind; he is free from cause and free from fruit; he transcends Vairocana and surpasses Śākyamuni. Not...
Deceived by the causes and effects of ordinary beings and sages, no one anywhere recognizes you. Do you understand?
Do not merely remain attached to the net of love within birth and death; you will be bound and carried away by good and evil karma, leaving you with no freedom.

Even if you refine your body and mind until they are as empty as space, even if you reach the state of brilliant clarity and profound stillness, you have not transcended the *vijñāna-skandha* (the aggregate of consciousness). Ancient...
People call this a "swift-flowing stream. Because the flow is so rapid, one does not realize it and falsely deems it tranquil.

Practicing in such a manner, one will never be able to transcend the boundaries of saṃsāra; as before, one will continue to be carried away by the cycle of birth and death. Therefore it is said: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
Even the fruits and accomplishments of the Three Vehicles are thus to be feared. Without the eye of the Way, they are likewise not ultimate. How could they compare to—?
Now, you ordinary people of this vast world do not need to expend even a hair’s breadth of effort to suddenly transcend;
can you understand and save your mental energy? Do you still aspire to this? I exhort you: I shall stand here now and wait for you to grasp it;
I will no longer require you to apply further effort or refine your practice through asceticism. If you do not act thus now, when else will you? Will you consent? Then he descended from his seat.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "All of you are like those sitting at the bottom of the ocean; submerged head-first and drenched, you still stretch out your hands to ask others for water to drink.
Now, a Bodhisattva who studies Prajñā must possess a great vessel and have great wisdom before they can succeed.
If one possesses wisdom, one may escape right this very moment. But if one's faculties are dull and slow, one must simply..."
Exert yourself with diligence and endurance; day and night, forget your fatigue. Be as if you had lost your parents—sleepless and losing your appetite.

With such urgency, spend your entire life to it. If you can further receive the support of another, investigating until the very marrow and reaching the ultimate reality, it will not be difficult to grasp.
Moreover, who nowadays is truly capable of receiving instruction? O worthy one, do not merely memorize words.
A recorded saying: It was as if he were reciting a *dhāraṇī*. He stepped forward with his feet while making "tō-tō" and "hō-hō" sounds in his mouth.
When someone seized him and questioned him, he had no way to escape and became angry, saying: "The Master does not answer my questions!
Practicing Zen like this is truly bitter! Do you understand? There is a certain kind of monk who sits upon a rope-bench and claims to be "well-knowing."
As for consciousness: when questioned, it immediately shakes its body and moves its hands; it rolls its eyes, sticks out its tongue, and stares blankly.

Furthermore, there is another kind that speaks of "luminous clarity" and "spiritual intelligence," claiming that this conscious nature of the spiritual platform is capable of seeing and hearing, acting as the sovereign within the field of the five aggregates.
To act as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) in such a manner is to greatly deceive people. Do you understand? I now ask you:
if you recognize this brilliant and lucid awareness as your true self, why is it not brilliant and lucid when you are drowsy?
If it is not [yourself] when you are drowsy, then why is there this brilliance and lucidity at other times? Do you understand yet? This is called...
To mistake a thief for one's own son is the very root of birth and death; it is the breath of delusive thought. Do you wish to know the origin of this root?
I have said that its luminous clarity arises solely from the discrimination of external objects, such as forms, sounds, and fragrances.

He then said, "This is what is called 'luminous and numinous. If there were no external objects before you, this luminosity and numinosity of yours would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit. O worthy one, where does true reality reside?
If you now wish to attain mastery over the field of the five aggregates, you need only recognize your own secret vajra-body. The ancients told you: it is the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected nature)."
It is perfectly pervasive, encompassing the entire realm of sand-grains. I shall now provide you with a brief explanation; the wise may attain understanding through analogy.
Do you still see the sun over Jambudvīpa in the south? It is that by which people in the world perform their activities, providing nourishment and sustaining their bodies and lives.
All various mental activities and karmic actions are established by relying upon the light of the sun. But does the essence of the sun itself possess many kinds of mental activities?
Does it have any place where it is not all-pervasive? If you wish to recognize the adamantine essence, you must likewise view it in this way:
right now, the mountains, rivers, and great earth; the lands of the ten directions; form and emptiness, light and darkness—and as for you...
Body and mind are entirely sustained by the manifestation of your perfected majestic radiance.

Indeed, this is the sequence of karmic actions performed by the various classes of human beings and all living creatures, and the resulting fruits of rebirth they receive. Whether sentient or insentient, none fail to sustain themselves through your majestic radiance.
Even the Buddhas’ attainment of enlightenment and their reception of beings to benefit them—all is entirely sustained by your majestic radiance. It is precisely like the adamantine essence.
Furthermore, are there ordinary beings and Buddhas? Since you possess such a marvelous capacity for manifesting yourself in the presence of reality, why do you not bring this forth and realize it?
Why instead do you follow others, making your living within the ghost-realm of the field of the five aggregates, deceiving yourself directly?
Suddenly, when the demon of impermanence arrives, your eyes will roll back in terror and your body will fall into the view of self-existence.
I command you to see this: at such a time, it is extremely difficult to sustain and bear. It is like a living tortoise shedding its shell; it is great suffering.
O worthy one, do not take a drowsy understanding and pass it off as sufficient. You have not yet been able to cover even a hair’s breadth.
Do you understand? There is no peace in the three realms; they are like a burning house. Furthermore, you are not yet a person who has attained peace and joy. Only...
Forming great crowds, you interfere in the affairs of others, flying and running here and there like wild deer; you seek only food and clothing.
If you act in this manner, how can you practice the Way of the King? Do you know? Neither kings nor great ministers shall restrain you.
Your parents have permitted you to leave the household life; donors from the ten directions provide you with food and clothing; and the local spirits and dragons protect you.
You must possess a sense of shame and gratitude before you may succeed. Do not fail these people. On this long bed, you sit in rows with your feet touching the ground, wasting away as time passes.
To say it is peaceful and happy is premature; it is all merely that you are being sustained by rice gruel and meals.
It is like a rotting winter melon; it will change and be taken away, or be buried in the earth. One’s karmic consciousness is vast and empty, with no foundation to rely upon.
Why has the śramaṇa come to such a state? As for all those wriggling creatures upon the great earth, I call them those dwelling through kalpas in hell.
If you do not resolve this now, tomorrow or the day after, you will enter the womb of a donkey or a horse.
Dragging plows and pulling harrows; carrying iron loads and saddles; being pounded by pestles and ground by mills;
being burned and boiled in water and fire—it is truly not easy to endure. You must be filled with great dread! This is your own doing; do you understand?
If you were to realize it, from the very beginning throughout eternal kalpas, I would never have let you have this news. If you do not realize it, these afflictions and evil karmic causes...
These conditions will not come to rest after one or two kalpas; they shall endure for as long as your adamantine essence. Do you understand? Ascending the hall, he said:
"The true school of the ancient Buddhas constantly manifests in accordance with things. Its majestic application appears everywhere, its radiance flowing forth in every place.
Manifestation and concealment are equanimous; high and low are fully illumined. Therefore, the superior śramaṇa takes the eye of the Way as primary, realizing the fundamental clarity."
The mind alone is the ultimate reality. The myriad phenomena of the universe share a single source; they are vast and boundless—whom would there be to speak of as being obstructed?
The events of kalpas past are all present before one’s eyes. Yet, because people of today are distanced by the passage of time, they deviate from their original nature.

Confused in mind, they identify with external objects and thus turn their backs on the True Source. Clinging to existence or stagnating in emptiness, they fail to encounter virtuous friends or fellow practitioners, remaining instead mired in self-interest.
The mind forms interpretations; even if there is deliberation, it remains entirely within the realm of conceptualization.

When one reaches the ground where principle is sought to its ultimate limit, one cannot distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox—how much less so when, throughout one's life, one has never personally investigated this for oneself? As for the former sages and ancient worthies, they naturally knew the proper time.

To overcome oneself is the only true merit. Regarding the cave-dwelling hermits of ancient times, a former sage said: "If the mind retains the measure of the sages, one still falls into the dust of dharmas;

if self-view is not yet forgotten, it results in leakage. One must not merely observe fasts and uphold precepts, sit constantly without lying down, arbitrarily contemplate emptiness, or concentrate the spirit to enter meditative absorption;
even if you do these things, you will simply depart [from the truth]. What connection can there be? Even the non-Buddhist outsiders of the Western Heavens can enter such states.

For eighty thousand kalpas, they remain fixed in concentration, their spirits stilled and tranquil; they close their eyes and hide their pupils, extinguishing their physical form and ceasing their intellect.

Yet, when these kalpas have run their course, they cannot escape the cycle of birth and death. This is because their eye of the Way is not clear and the root-source of birth and death has not been severed.

Those who have left the household life are not like this; they must not be equated with those heterodox outsiders. They must, indeed, possess true and penetrating realization, endowed with great wisdom and vision.
One can penetrate together with all Buddhas; in silent illumination, knowing is forgotten. Emptily containing the myriad images, right now, where is there that is not you?
Where is there that is not clear? Where is there that is not manifest? Why do you not understand it in this way?
If you do not block this field, how can you withstand the various leakages that arise during daily life? Everything will become empty and false.
Who, then, is the one who has attained the place of strength throughout their life? If you have not yet realized this according to reality, you must be urgent.
During your time, forget food and lose sleep; act as if your head were on fire, as if you had lost your very life. With a darkened mind, save yourself by casting aside all distractions.
Only when the mind and consciousness are brought to rest will there be a slight degree of intimacy.
If it is not so, then tomorrow or the day after, everything will be carried away by discursive consciousness; what freedom will there be? Now, however, these insentient things are superior to us;
they proclaim clearly and distinctly. Earth, wood, stone, and pebbles preach the Dharma with extraordinary truthfulness—there is simply no one to hear them.
One must be able to listen; only upon hearing this teaching can one begin to deliberate. But tell me, how does one deliberate on the Dharma spoken by the insentient?
Try to say it. One cannot say there is no speaking and no discourse, nor that there is no seeing and no listening.
Nor can one say that it is spoken of itself without being asked, praising the path one practices. Have you not seen how the youth Sudhana visited fifty [patriarchs]?

These three people were spiritual friends; at the very end, they beheld Maitreya. In the mere twinkling of an eye, they entered the gate. As soon as they had entered, the gate closed of its own accord.
Within the multi-storied pavilion, they beheld hundreds of thousands of Buddhas undergoing the process of casting off one body and receiving another throughout the past.
The one hundred and twenty spiritual friends he had visited all appeared simultaneously within the pavilion to serve as witnesses for him.
Sudhana’s doubts were instantly stilled. Generally speaking, if one can fully reveal this reality beneath the three rafters, it may then be discussed:
that within the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence, one is identical to the pure lands of all Buddhas. Furthermore...
Why fear birth and death? Furthermore, who knows that all dharmas are entirely devoid of substantial reality?
At the assembly on Vulture Peak, Kāśyapa heard this directly, yet it was like discussing the moon. An ancient worthy said: "Do not deliberate upon good or evil at all."

It is just like pointing at the moon. Even the practices, stages, and liberations of the Three Vehicles, the nirvāṇa of bodhisattvas, and the holy virtues and fruits of the sages are all like flowers in the sky or the horns of a rabbit. Not seeing the Way, one returns to contemplate the world as if it were a dream;
conditioned mental phenomena cannot be relied upon. As days and years pass, they yield no benefit whatsoever, for they only involve turning away from the Truth and abandoning it.
Fundamentally, you harbor a weary detachment from ordinary sentiments and direct your mind toward the holy path; yet this understanding of yours does not transcend the limitations of others.

You cast aside the five aggregates but fail to depart from them; you do not see that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are laws of arising and ceasing. You merely intend to move forward.
Only those capable of clear realization can penetrate through to the core; only then will they know it.

If you have not yet investigated it thoroughly, you should know that all of this is mere empty talk—a teaching difficult for the world to believe. Only those endowed with great capacity can clearly comprehend it.

If you penetrate it in this life, it will remain so for ten thousand kalpas. As the ancient masters said: "One must resolve it directly in this very life; who could endure undergoing it through successive kalpas?"
The remaining karmic retribution.
Take care. [Ascending the hall: The sun-wheel in the great void is that by which all people are established; the great void is present now.

Yet how is it that you all, though looking with eyes full before you, do not see it, and though listening with ears full before you, do not hear it? If you fail to realize these two points, it is nothing other than deluded sleep.
If one attains clear penetration, one sits transcending both ordinary beings and sages; one sits transcending the triple world.

This dream-like, illusory body and mind do not contain so much as a single thing the size of a needle’s eye to serve as a condition or an object of perception. Even if all the Buddhas were to appear and manifest infinite supernatural powers and transformations, [it would remain thus].
Even with so many nets of teaching, not a single hair’s breadth has been applied; they merely serve as a gateway for beginners to cultivate faith. Do you understand?
The waterbirds and forest trees can actually grasp the essential thread. How precise they are! It is simply that few people listen; it is no small matter.

For celestial demons and heterodox paths to act thus would be to betray kindness and violate righteousness; for devas, humans, and those in the six realms of existence to do so would be to [betray their own nature].
Deceiving oneself and deluding others—nowadays, these śramaṇas do not realize this matter; instead, they become men who merely dally with shadows.
Floating and sinking within the sea of birth and death, when will they ever find rest? Fortunately, you yourselves possess such a vast and magnificent tradition, yet you are unable to inherit it.
Instead, you seek to act as masters within the field of the five aggregates. The great earth cannot support you, and empty space cannot contain you.
"It is exhaustive. How could this be a small matter? If you wish to penetrate thoroughly, then right here and now you must attain clear penetration.
I do not instruct you to take up a single dharma as large as a speck of dust; I do not instruct you to discard a single dharma as small as a hair. Do you understand?
At that time, a monk asked, "What is the fundamental principle of the ancestors? The Master remained silent. The monk asked again, and the Master then shouted at him.
A monk asked, "By what gate of skillful means can you cause students to enter? The Master said, "Entering is itself the skillful means.
The monk asked, "When a person with a beginner's mind comes, how do you instruct them? The Master said, "From where have you obtained this 'beginner's mind'?
The monk asked, "I am a student newly entering the monastic community; I beg the Master for guidance and support. The Master pointed at him with his staff. The monk said, "I, your student..."
"No," the Master said. "If I were to act for you in this way, it would instead result in my suppressing and demeaning you.

Now, if you truly accept [the truth] for yourself, then from your own perspective—whether you are a beginner entering the monastic community or one who has long trodden the path with others—you will lack nothing compared to the Buddhas of the past.
You will be like the waters of the great ocean, where all fish and dragons, from their first birth until old age [find their sustenance]."
In inhaling and exhaling, in receiving and enjoying, all are entirely equal. Therefore it is said: "The one who first resolves their mind stands shoulder-to-shoulder with the Buddhas of antiquity.
Yet alas, throughout beginningless eons, you have stirred various deluded sentiments, binding them into afflictions.

Like a gravely ill person whose mind is frantic, feverish, and distressed, your inverted and chaotic views are devoid of any reality whatsoever. All the objective realms perceived at this moment are likewise [empty].
It is also like this. In relation to your various sense faculties, everything has become inverted.

The ancients used inexhaustible, wondrous medicines to treat and counteract this, yet they did not attain clarity until reaching the tenth stage (*bhūmi*). From this, one knows that [enlightenment] is no small matter. The ancients reflected upon this.
It is as if you had lost your parents; it is like brothers today who see one another as if by chance. Where else is there anyone who can resolve this for you?

It is a pity that your time is being wasted in vain. Why not investigate this yourself in secret, examining it with great care until you reach the point where there is no effort to be made, and all conditions naturally subside?
Even if the sprout has not yet emerged, the seed still remains. If you grasp at me entirely...
Beating drums at the neighbor’s house and expending the energy required for preparing gruel—using such haste to try to cast off birth and death is merely a deception that wastes a lifetime;
what benefit is there in it? You must understand and grasp this according to reality. There is nothing more to do. Take care.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "O worthy ones, at this time, having no other recourse, I am forced to suppress such majestic radiance and offer bitter-mouthed exhortations through hundreds of thousands of skillful means—whether in this way or that—to share my understanding with you.
Yet all of it results in inverted views. With these throats, lips, and mouths, I have only achieved the karma of a wild fox spirit to deceive you. Will you accept this?"
"Ma! As for whether there is fault or no fault, only I know it myself; how could you possibly understand?
If someone like this were to come forward, they would willingly submit to my reprimand. Truly, being a master is not easy at all;
one must be a true *kalyāṇamitra* (virtuous friend) before succeeding. Even though I am now using such expedient means to assist you, you still cannot grasp it."
Zhongchun raises the essential vehicle: "Where will you place this? Do you understand? Forty-nine years were but expedient means. Consider this:
at the assembly on Vulture Peak, there were a million followers, yet only Kāśyapa alone heard it directly;
all the others did not hear it. Tell me, what is that which Kāśyapa heard directly? You cannot say it was like...
Coming, there is no speaking of speech; Kāśyapa hears what is not heard, and he shall immediately depart.
This cannot be the matter of your cultivating causes to achieve results—the adornment of merit and wisdom. Do you understand?

For instance, when it is said that Dagu entrusted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to Mahākāśyapa, I say it is like talking about the moon. Caoxi’s raising of the whisk is likewise like pointing at the moon. Therefore—
The Way. Within the Great Tang Empire, regarding the matters of the Vehicle of the Patriarchs, I have never seen a single person who has raised it up and proclaimed it.

Even if there were someone to raise it up and proclaim it, all the people of the entire earth would lose their lives; it would be like an unperforated iron hammer, causing everyone at once to lose their edge and be rendered tongue-tied.
You all are fortunate to have encountered me, for I do not spare my own life or body as I share with you this inverted knowledge and vision.
"Follow your own wild mind; only then will there be a place for you to pose questions.
If I did not allow you to know and hear me in this way, where would you ever find me? Do you understand? It is a great difficulty. Exert yourself! Be careful!"

Ascending the hall, he said: "All of you see danger and evil; you see tigers, swords, and various such things threatening your lives, and thus you give rise to boundless fear. What is this like? It is exactly like a worldly painter."
I once painted a depiction of the transformations of hell; having finished the tigers, swords, and blades, I looked at them intently and was suddenly struck with fear and terror myself.
You people here today are just like this: you perceive all manner of things as existing, yet these are merely the illusions projected by yourselves.
You naturally give rise to fear and dread, yet it is not another person who has brought this fault upon you. Do you now wish to awaken from this illusory delusion?
Simply recognize your own adamantine eye. If you recognize it, I have never taught that there is even a speck of dust that can be manifested;
where else could there be tigers, wolves, swords, or blades to threaten and intimidate you? Even until the time of Śākyamuni...
Even with such skillful means, one cannot find a place to emerge. Therefore, I told you: "The śramaṇa’s eye grasps the world;
it encompasses heaven and earth without leaking so much as a hair’s breadth. Where else could there be a single thing for you to perceive?
Do you understand? Such is the liberation; such is the marvel! Why do you not investigate and grasp it?
When the Master ascended the hall after a long time, the assembly all assumed he would not preach the Dharma and each returned at once. The Master then rebuked them, saying:
"Look at this lot; they are all of one kind. Not a single one possesses wisdom. They merely see me opening these two flaps of skin."
They all come crowding around, seeking words and conjectures, yet they do not realize at all that I am acting for their true benefit.
Look at this! It is truly difficult, truly difficult.

The Master lamented that the Great Dharma is difficult to uphold and that those of superior capacity are rarely encountered. Students rely on words to produce understanding, yet they lose the essential point by following their own perceptions.
He then revealed the three phrases of the fundamental principle, saying: "As for the first phrase, simply take responsibility for yourself. It is already fully present and complete;
throughout the entire ten directions of the world, there is nothing else. It is merely you yourself. Who else is there to see? Who else is there to hear? It is all, without exception, this."
Whatever your mind-king does, it is entirely the perfection of immovable wisdom (*acala-jñāna*). It merely lacks your own personal acceptance of it.

This is called "opening the door of skillful means" to lead you to believe that there is a portion of true permanence flowing on, which has been so from the beginningless past through to the present, never not being so and never not being otherwise.
However, this statement only establishes the dharma of equality. Why? Because it merely uses words to dispel [delusions].
He said: "To pursue principle with principle is merely to accord with the ordinary nature and characteristics of things in order to interact with others and benefit sentient beings.

Yet, regarding the fundamental tenet, this still clarifies what precedes but not what follows; it is called 'one-flavor' and 'plain reality. It is but the measure of partial realization of the Dharma-body, lacking any phrase that transcends the conventional.
One dies beneath the words and has no share in true freedom. If one knows how to transcend these measures, one will not be bound by the mind."
Sent by Māra, it enters into one’s hands and is immediately transformed, falling step by step. To say this "penetrates the Great Way" is to fall into the view of ordinary equanimity;

therefore, this is called the first phrase of the fundamental principle (*jiaozong*). The second phrase: returning the cause to accord with the fruit, one does not cling to the principle of ordinary oneness (*yiru*).
This expedient means is called "shifting positions to meet the occasion," where life and death are sovereign, and one freely bestows or withdraws.
Acting according to what is appropriate, one enters birth and death to extensively benefit all beings, utterly transcending the realms of form, desire, attachment, and views.

This expedient means is called the Buddha-nature that suddenly surmounts the three realms. This is termed the simultaneous clarification of two principles and the concurrent illumination of two meanings;
it is not moved by the two extremes, and its wondrous function manifests before one. This is called the governing principle of the second phrase. Third...

This passage reveals the fundamental nature and characteristics of great wisdom. It penetrates insights that transcend measure, illuminating the yin and penetrating the yang, expanding throughout the entire dharma-realm.
Within this single true essence, the great function manifests before one; its responsive transformations are boundless, such that it is entirely functional and yet entirely non-functional.
The total preservation of life and the total non-arising of birth—this expedient means is called the gate of the samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*).
This is what is termed the third sentence of the fundamental tenet. *Xuansha Yulu*, Middle Volume.
The Master gave this instruction: "The veteran masters of all quarters all say they 'receive things and benefit living beings.
But as for these three kinds of sick people—how do you receive them? The one suffering from blindness: you raise the mallet or brandish the whisk, yet he does not see.

The one suffering from deafness: you speak the samādhi of words, yet he does not hear. The one suffering from muteness: you try to teach him to speak, yet he cannot speak. If you cannot receive them..."

[The Master] said, "It is so. The Buddha-dharma has no spiritual efficacy. At that time, a monk came forward and said, "Regarding the three types of sick people, do you permit this student to offer a discussion?
The Master said, "I permit it. [The monk asked,] "How would you discuss them? The monk then bowed respectfully and departed. The Master said, "That was not it."
"Not so," the Arhat said. "Guishen currently possesses eyes, ears, and a mouth; how will you, Master, receive him?
The Master said, "I am ashamed," and immediately returned to his quarters. Zhongta said, "Where are these three types of sick people now?
Another monk said, "Not only do they deceive him, but they also deceive themselves."
Fayan said, "When I heard that monk being pointed out by the Arhat at that time, I immediately understood the three types of sick people.
Yunju Xi said, "As for this monk—did he understand or not? If you say he understood, Xuansha also said it was not so.
If you say he did not understand, why did Fayan say, 'Because of this monk's words, I [understood]...'"?
There were three types of patients present. The Elder had no ailment; this has been discussed above for those who wish to know.
Yunju Yuan said: "Dizang is like a dragon without horns; Xuansha is like a snake with feet. Xuansha has only the vanguard, but lacks the rearguard.
Both men’s illnesses have reached the vital organs (gao-huang), beyond the reach of acupuncture or medicine. Shan [said]: "..."
The Master [Yunmen] broke it open for you all: holding up his staff, he said, "The eye upon the tip of the staff is as bright as the sun;
if you wish to recognize true gold, look for it within the fire. A monk requested instruction from Yunmen. Yunmen said, "Prostrate yourself."
The monk rose to prostrate. Yunmen poked him with his staff; as the monk stepped back, Yunmen said, "Are you not blind?
He called him forward again. As the monk approached, Yunmen said, "Are you not deaf?
Yunmen asked, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not. Yunmen said, "Are you not mute? At this, the monk attained realization.
[The Master] paused. After Xuedou Xian had finished citing [the story], he gave a shout and said: "This blind, deaf, and mute fellow!
Had it not been for Yunmen, he would have been lost for donkey years. Nowadays, some people either pick up a mallet or brandish a whisk, yet he pays them no mind;
they tell him to come closer, yet he does not come. Do you understand? He does not respond to anyone anywhere—how can one deal with him?"
"Ma! If Xuedou had not been able to deal with it, what would you lot—this team of donkeys—be good for?
With his staff, he drove them all away at once. Benjue said, "Yunmen and Xuedou were like blowing fire with the wind or releasing a hawk upon seeing a rabbit;
how could they compare to Dizang’s waves against the current? At that time, having heard Xuansha—"
Having spoken thus, he stepped out from the assembly and said, "I have eyes, I have ears, and I have a mouth; I pray the Master will receive me.

Xuan Sha said, "How shameful! and then let out a great laugh. Not only Xuan Sha—indeed, all the Buddhas and Patriarchs of India and this land would have been forced to withdraw when subjected to such a pressure. Suddenly, he took up his staff and said:
"To let this pass would be unacceptable. Jingshan Daokai said, "Although this monk has indeed attained awakening, he has only awakened to Yunmen Chan.
As for Xuansha Chan, he must buy more straw sandals and travel on foot again. Tiantong Huiming said:
Yunmen spreads it out flat; this monk truly repays him. But tell me, where is the point of awakening for this monk?
When a disease is incurable, it is difficult to apply acupuncture or moxibustion. Longmen Yuan said: "Good brother, do you know the true way of acting?
Today, I shall not spare my eyebrows to explain it through for all of you. It is just like when you people..."
As for the two eyes, when have they ever seen anything? As for the two ears, when have they ever heard anything? As for the mouth, when has it ever spoken anything?
Since there is no speaking, no hearing, and no seeing, where can there be such things as forms, sounds, odors, or tastes?
Although it is so, how many people can reach such a state? Verse: Blind, deaf, mute, and utterly beyond the reach of intellectual effort;
throughout heaven and earth, there is only laughter and sorrow. Even Li Zhu [the legendary master of vision] cannot...
Distinguishing the true colors: How could Master Kuang have recognized the dark threads? It is better to sit alone beneath a window of emptiness;
when the leaves fall and the flowers bloom, they do so of their own accord. He said again: "Do you understand? An unperforated iron hammer. (Xuedou Xian)
Retreating and then drawing near, engaging in debate face-to-face; meeting by chance, it is difficult to turn one's back. A spring breeze suddenly shakes the courtyard before us;
once again we see tens of thousands of falling petals. (Baizhang Yuanwen)
The Old Man Yunmen was one whose hands and eyes were intimately familiar [with the Way]; he fanned the fire with the wind without expending any effort.
The blind could see, and the deaf could hear. Although there were no words hanging upon his lips, it was a single Dharma-gate for three kinds of patients. (Fujian Qin).
The blind, the deaf, the mute, and the speech-impaired cannot receive it; Xuan Sha has wasted his efforts in vain.
Bian Que and Lu Yi fold their hands and retreat; all three suffer from terminal illnesses. (Gushan Gui)
Xuan Sha’s words on the three types of sick people transcend Yunmen’s "the six are not caught.
Do not wait for right and wrong to enter your ears; those who knew you before will turn into enemies. (Jingshan Daoyuan)
Wuquan manifests deafness, blindness, muteness, illness, and paralysis; yet he seeks to reveal our school and verify the master craftsmen.
A vajra cuts through iron as if crushing mud; once the golden thread is moved, Xuansha is lost. (Fenyang Shao)

If you wish to know the three kinds of people: their application of principle is ever fresh. There has never been even a hair’s breadth of a dharma that can act as a defilement for the inner or outer self. (Yongming Shou)
One, two, three. Seeing, hearing, and perceiving—who is this? Suddenly they are melted away. Where the flowers cluster, the partridges cry;
when the grass is fragrant, the mandarin ducks fly. Old Xuansha! Old Xuansha! Fortunately, he lacked one move at that time.
His words of ultimate truth are merely "so be it. In the midst of it all, half the tree’s fruit has fallen. (Cuiyan Zhen)
Xuan Sha’s three ways of receiving people are still present before the eyes and ears of all; there is no need to open one's eyes and wet the bed.
In vain, mountains are moved and seas are blocked. Amidst the flowers, the secluded bird sings without ceasing; the springtime radiance fills the earth—who will buy it?
(Anointed Poisoned Whip).
Xuan Sha’s three types of sick people: the principle does not lie in a loud voice.
This drew forth Old Man Xiangyan, who came to hang himself from a tree. (Longmen Yuan).
Xuansha used poison to expel the poison of others; three types of sick people were in one room. How laughable is the old, ancient sage Yunmen!
He lost his money in the river and went into the river to fish for it. (Oran’s Verse).
The blind, the deaf, and the mute have no concern with one another; do not allow yourself to be deceived by Xuansha’s reckless flattery.
I shall reveal a single phrase for you once more: the Old Lord wears a crown of mulberry bark, obscuring the empty clarity.
Deaf, blind, mute, and dumb—caught and defeated! What more can be asked? Deaf, blind, mute, and dumb. (Yuelin Guan) He employed various expedient means to test those who are true masters.
Who has personally seen Old Xuansha? His ears are deaf, his mouth is mute, and his eyes are blind.
The sentient beings of the five turbidities are as numerous as hemp seeds. (Hengchuan Gong)
Xuefeng ascended the hall and said, "To understand this matter is like an ancient mirror set upon its stand: when a barbarian comes, it reflects the barbarian;
when a Han Chinese comes, it reflects the Han Chinese. The Master asked, "What happens when a bright mirror comes? Xuefeng said, "Both barbarian and Han Chinese are hidden.
The Master said, "Old monk, your feet have not yet touched the ground."

While the Master was in the midst of his formal session, he heard the sound of a swallow and said, "He speaks deeply of the true nature of reality; he skillfully expounds the essentials of the Dharma.
He then descended from his seat. At that time, a monk requested further instruction, saying, "I do not understand. The Master replied, "Go away! Who would believe you?"

Verse: The purple swallow flies back to circle the painted beams; Deeply discussing the true nature (*dharmatā*), its resonance flows on and on. Of a thousand words and ten thousand phrases, no one understands;
It follows the warbling oriole over the low wall once more. (Fundamental Enlightenment I)

In my humble official service, I have hurried north and south; for long I have pined for the dust of the traveler's road. Amidst the misty rain and smoke, I deeply recall the spring of my old garden. (By Yan Shouhui)
Killing and giving life race against one another; for a thousand *li* they do not share the same view. One might save the eyebrows, yet lose the nostrils. (Kōsoku In).
When the King of Min sent lychees to the Master, the Master held one up and showed it to the assembly, saying:
"This lychee is so red! This lychee is so crimson! How do you all understand this? If you say it is 'one color'..."
This is a clumsy way of speaking. If you say it is the various colors, you again fall into the extremes of annihilationism or eternalism. How will you all handle this?
A monk stepped forward and said, "One must not fail to recognize the *lìzhī* (lychee). The Master, acting as his representative, said, "It is simply the *lìzhī*."

The *Zhizhengchuan* states: "To dispel words with words, and to dispel principles with principles, are both merely the circulation of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and cannot constitute the seeing of the Way.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "It is like using one wedge to extract another. As Xuan Sha once said:
"A student should employ the pivot that does not shift in the midst of activity. Yet, even those who have spent their lives in the monastic groves fail to recognize these words—how lamentable!
Xuan Sha once ate lychees and asked the assembly, "This lychee is so red; this lychee is so crimson.
How do you all account for this? If you say it is a single color, that is still a state of stagnation.
If you say it consists of many colors, you merely fall into the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism. So, how will you all handle this?"
Shengyan said, "It is simply that you, Master, must clarify this for yourself. Xuansha said, "This is a muddled and foolish state;
what connection does it have [to the truth]? Chongji said, "In the end, it is all just a single color.
Xuansha said, "If everyone is so muddled, when will there ever be an end? He then turned back and asked Jiaoran, "How would you say it?"
Jiaoran said, "One must not fail to recognize the *lǜzhī* (lychee). Xuansha said, "It is simply a *lǜzhī*.
He further said, "All of you have been here with me for so long, yet you all speak in this manner; you do not distinguish between the black and the white."
"You do not recognize auspiciousness or inauspiciousness. I have recently been telling you that the point of application is an unchanging pivot;
why then do you merely engage in dialogue? What connection is there [between this and the truth]? Master Xianyan said:

'The former sages took pity on your inverted pursuits and provided a single phrase to bring about liberation. If you understand such matters as these, cast them aside in a state of ease and settle yourself.'"
With a modicum of physical strength, he instead answers with a "pivot-word" (*huatou*) from a witty remark and treats it as the Way of Chan;
not only does he deceive himself, but he also deceives others.
Once, while walking along a bamboo fence with Xuefeng, the Master asked, "Is there any Buddha-dharma even here where we walk along this fence? Xuefeng said:
[Daowei] said, "There is. The Master asked, "What is the Buddha-dharma of the interlaced fence? Feng shook the fence once. The Master said, "I do not do it that way.
Feng asked, "How would you do it? The Master said, "It comes right through the bamboo strips."
The Master took his leave of Xuefeng, saying, "I inform the Abbot: every person is free and at ease. I am now going down the mountain.
Xuefeng asked, "Who says such a thing? The Master said, "It is you, the Abbot, who say such a thing.
Xuefeng asked, "How about you? The Master said, "I am not free and at ease. Xuefeng said, "I know."
Changqing arrived. The Master asked, "Setting aside the medicinal taboos, how do you speak? Changqing said, "Why are you being so foolish?
The Master said, "Picking acorns on Xuefeng Mountain, you come here to let the sparrows drop their dung."
The Master, because a monk had prostrated, said: "It is because of me that you may prostrate. Verse:
"You prostrate to me so that I may prostrate to you; I laugh at myself for being devoid of principle. Is it only the venerable Xuansha? All people under heaven [are the same]."
It is so. (Juehaiyuan). Because of me, you are able to pay homage to me.
When fallen, I support you; when up, I support you again. If you wish to go, you may go immediately;
if you wish to stop, you may stop immediately. (Baofengming).
The Master did not recognize characters; Bodhidharma did not understand Chan. Xuan Sha never said such words—do not recklessly transmit them. (Jingshan Gao)
A sharp sword severs one’s own life-root; do not rely on grass or wood for support.
If you impart even a single dharma to another, you will forever enter the Hell of the Severed Tongue. (Gushan Gui)
"Because of me, you receive my prostrations. The ox is led away to drink water; on the bank, hoof meets hoof;
in the water, snout faces snout. (Gao'an Wu)
Because of me, you receive my prostration. Mount Kunlun lies at the bottom of the pool; though the waves beat against the heavens, there is not a drop of water upon his body. (Xuetang Xing)
"Because of me, you may receive my prostration. Be clearly and properly ashamed. Xuansha was not being foolish. Tsk!
Open your eyes and stop dozing off. (Zhaotang 1)
To speak of "you" and to speak of "me" is to fall into the trap of shifting views. All sentient beings in the great earth are originally not a single one.
(Dian-niu-you). A rat gnawing at raw iron—how distinct its flavor! A cat looking left and right—even swallowing saliva does not reach through. (Zheng-tang-bian).
"Because of me, you receive my prostrations. To exhaust the source, one must reach the bottom. Nine times nine is eighty-one. Yama, King of Hell, is but a ghost.
(Zhian Yan). (The *Yuan-yu* revises this to: "Right now, one returns home; there is no separation by even a single sheet of paper.")
It is because of me that you are being paid homage. All matters arise from instructions. Who would have known that the wind among white artemisia does not reside within the autumn river? (Tianmu Li)
"Because of me, you receive my prostrations. Do not let out flatulence or discharge excrement, thereby bringing trouble upon all people under heaven.
